query: For high-entropy alloys used in thermal-insulation applications, what testable hypothesis could be made about an unspecified predictive approach for accurately identifying materials with low phonon thermal conductivity? The hypothesis should explain why the approach would work, predict its improvement over current predictions, define its applicability limits, identify supporting evidence, and specify a decisive experimental benchmark and outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive approach that explicitly incorporates advanced descriptors of lattice distortion and force‐constant fluctuations—quantified by measures of atomic disorder—in high-entropy alloys will more accurately identify materials with low phonon thermal conductivity compared to conventional methods that use only averaged properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase, compositionally random high-entropy alloys (such as FeCoCrMnNi-like systems) exhibiting severe lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Apply an expanded predictive method (e.g., an enhanced machine learning or simulation framework) that transforms raw compositional data into descriptors capturing force-constant fluctuation magnitudes and local lattice distortions.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be conducted under conditions where the single-phase state persists (e.g., room temperature and moderate elevated temperatures) and the phonon behavior is dominant for heat transport.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations (estimated around 20–50% variability) arising from the intrinsic chemical randomness of high-entropy alloys.
generation.mechanism: The severe lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations enhance phonon scattering, thereby reducing the lattice thermal conductivity. The predictive method, by including these descriptors, captures this scattering mechanism better than models based on averaged structural features.
generation.predicted_outcome: The predictive approach will identify high-entropy alloys with lower phonon thermal conductivity, improving the prediction accuracy (directionally by an estimated 10–20% improvement over traditional methods) as validated by experimental measurements of phonon dynamics and lattice thermal conductivity.
generation.baseline: Current prediction methods based on average atomic properties or binary alloy analogues yield broader error margins and less accurate κ_L estimations in high-entropy systems.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be effective primarily in single-phase, statistically random high-entropy alloys. It may not apply to multiphase systems or alloys where electronic contributions dominate the thermal conduction.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement (e.g., 10–20%) is uncertain until sufficient benchmarking data across multiple high-entropy alloy systems is available.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize and characterize a series of single-phase high-entropy alloys chosen by the predictive model to possess low phonon thermal conductivity. Measure the phonon dispersion and lattice thermal conductivity using techniques such as inelastic neutron scattering (or Raman spectroscopy) and laser flash analysis, respectively, under relevant temperature conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental measurements of κ_L and phonon scattering characteristics consistently deviate from the predictions—specifically, if alloys predicted to exhibit low κ_L do not show significantly reduced thermal conductivity compared to traditional methods—the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Recently, entropy engineering has been used as a novel strategy to optimize the electrical and thermal transport properties of TE materials. By increasing element species, the mixing entropy in a material system increases quickly, and high-entropy materials with over five principal elements will be formed. Severe lattice distortion is usually the core phenomenon of high-entropy material—such distortion leads to strong scattering for heat-carrying phonons and results in low lattice thermal conductivity. Stabilizing single-phase structures by increasing entropy weakens the phase-boundary electron scattering in multiphase high-entropy material, thus providing a beneficial contribution to improve electrical transport properties, i.e., entropy-driven structural stabilization,. Therefore, the high-entropy-stabilized composition should work as a good matrix for further optimization of TE performance by integrating the traditional optimization strategy.

In conclusion, we have reported the first experimental investigation of the acoustic phonon dispersions in a High-Entropy Alloy, complemented by the GVDOS survey, at room and low temperature. FeCoCrMnNi is a 5-element random alloy, and, despite the inherent disorder, its phonon dynamics closely resemble that of the pure elements composing it and the corresponding binary alloys. More specifically, acoustic phonons disperse throughout the whole Brillouin zone up to energies between 20 and 30 meV, exhibiting an attenuation stronger than in simple elements, but of the same order of magnitude as in binary alloys. The whole attenuation behavior can be understood in terms of scattering from force-constant fluctuations, which have been estimated to amount to ~20% using a simple theoretical model, a value comparable with calculations of Mu and co-authors on binary and ternary alloys made of the same elements. cited_evidence.text: Using the same approach, the value of κL was computed for various temperatures in the range 300–700 K (Figure 9). At 300 K, the κL value is 0.4 W K−1 m−1, which is a very low value of the lattice thermal conductivity, favorable for thermoelectric materials. This is due to the lattice distortion effect of high-entropy alloys that can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low thermal conductivity. Additionally, one can observe that when the temperature rises, the thermal conductivity of the lattice decreases, which is also due to an increase in phonon scattering at higher temperatures.
